challenges.fact: An Jung-geun wrote a treatise on peace in East Asia while awaiting execution, calling for cooperation between China, Japan, and Korea against Western colonialism. He was a complex figure — a Catholic, a scholar, and a revolutionary.

challenges.statement: Ahn Jung-geun, who assassinated Japanese Resident-General Itō Hirobumi, was celebrated in Japan as well as Korea after his death.
challenges.fact: Ahn Jung-geun was executed by Japan in 1910. In Korea he is a national hero; in China, a statue stands at Harbin station where the assassination occurred. In Japan he is officially considered a criminal. The same act reads entirely differently across national histories.

challenges.question: Coco Chanel popularised which garment in 1926 that became a symbol of modern fashion?
challenges.fact: Chanel's 'little black dress' (1926) appeared in Vogue, which compared it to Ford's Model T — a fashion so universal and timeless it was available to everyone. Black had previously been reserved for mourning.

challenges.question: Arrange these milestones of Chanel's fashion revolution in chronological order:
items: Opens her first millinery shop in Paris — hats only, no corsets
Introduces jersey fabric into women's fashion, replacing stiff silk
Chanel No. 5 becomes the world's best-selling perfume
Launches the little black dress in Vogue — 'the Ford of fashion'
challenges.fact: Each of Chanel's innovations stripped away constraint. Jersey replaced stiff silk; cardigan suits replaced corsets; black replaced colour as the dominant fashion statement. She built freedom into fashion at a time when clothing was still architecture built to restrict women's bodies.

challenges.instruction: The Jazz Age inspired Chanel's Paris salon. Arrange the notes of a 1920s jazz phrase.
challenges.fact: Chanel thrived in the Jazz Age Paris of the 1920s — a world of Picasso, Stravinsky, Diaghilev, and Hemingway. She dressed the dancers of the Ballets Russes and set the aesthetic for an entire era.

challenges.question: Coco Chanel revolutionised women's fashion primarily by:
options: Introducing the first ready-to-wear clothing line
Replacing corsets and heavy skirts with comfortable jersey fabrics
Designing uniforms for the French military
challenges.fact: Chanel borrowed jersey — a stretchy fabric used for men's undergarments — and transformed it into women's suits and dresses. At a time when women's fashion was literally painful, her clothes allowed women to move freely. "Elegance is refusal," she said.

challenges.question: Shaw's 1913 play 'Pygmalion' was later adapted into which enormously successful musical?
challenges.fact: My Fair Lady (1956) ran for 2,717 performances on Broadway. Shaw famously wrote his own stage directions to prevent producers from adding a romantic happy ending.

challenges.instruction: Shaw was fascinated by Darwin and evolution. Classify these beaks as Darwin would — each adapted to a different food source.
challenges.fact: Shaw wrote 'Back to Methuselah' (1921), a five-play epic spanning from Adam and Eve to 31,920 AD. He was the only person to win both a Nobel Prize (1925) and an Academy Award (1938).

challenges.instruction: A Hungarian phonetics expert approaches Eliza Doolittle at the ambassador's party. What does he conclude?
challenges.fact: Shaw's irony: Eliza succeeds so perfectly that the expert concludes she must be foreign nobility — her English is too refined for a native. Class is performance, not origin.

challenges.statement: George Bernard Shaw intended Eliza Doolittle and Professor Higgins to end up romantically together.
challenges.fact: Shaw explicitly wrote that Eliza marries Freddy Eynsford-Hill, not Higgins. He was furious when stage productions implied a romance. His epilogue spells out that Higgins is too self-absorbed for love. The musical My Fair Lady contradicts Shaw's own ending.

challenges.question: Eisenstein pioneered 'intellectual montage' — using the collision of images to create:
options: Abstract ideas that neither shot contains alone
challenges.fact: Eisenstein believed that two images in sequence create a third meaning absent from either — as in the Kuleshov effect. A shot of a man's neutral face followed by soup suggests hunger; followed by a coffin suggests grief. Same face, different meanings.

challenges.instruction: Eisenstein's Odessa Steps sequence builds to a critical cut. Choose how he resolved it.
challenges.fact: Eisenstein's montage theory holds that meaning is created between shots, not within them. The Battleship Potemkin (1925) remains the most studied example of this principle.

challenges.instruction: Eisenstein's montage: juxtapose shots so no image repeats the same idea in the same context — meaning emerges between them. Fill the grid so each row, column, and 2×2 box contains 1–4 exactly once.
challenges.fact: Eisenstein's montage theory holds that meaning is created between shots, not within them. The Kuleshov effect proves it: the same neutral face, cut to food, reads as hunger; cut to a coffin, reads as grief. The Odessa Steps sequence in Battleship Potemkin (1925) remains the most studied example of this principle.

challenges.question: Sergei Eisenstein's theory of "montage" in filmmaking means:
options: Using only natural light instead of artificial lighting
Cutting between shots to create meaning that neither shot alone contains
Filming every scene in one continuous take
Synchronising music precisely to on-screen action
challenges.fact: Eisenstein showed that two images cut together produce a third meaning in the viewer's mind — greater than either image alone. His Battleship Potemkin (1925) Odessa Steps sequence influenced every action film ever made, from Hitchcock to The Godfather.

challenges.question: Amelia Earhart disappeared near which island during her 1937 round-the-world attempt?
challenges.fact: Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan disappeared on July 2, 1937, near tiny Howland Island in the Central Pacific — one of the most remote spots on Earth. They were never found. Her disappearance remains one of aviation's great mysteries.

challenges.instruction: Chart Earhart's course through the storm corridors over the Atlantic.
challenges.fact: In 1932, Earhart flew solo from Newfoundland to Northern Ireland in 14 hours 56 minutes — battling icing, storm turbulence, and a leaking fuel tank.

challenges.instruction: Earth's orbit is an ellipse. Earhart circled the globe — calculate the area of the elliptical flight path around the equator.
challenges.fact: Earhart flew her Lockheed Electra around the world's equator — the longest possible circumnavigation route. She completed 22,000 miles before disappearing with only 7,000 miles remaining.

challenges.statement: Amelia Earhart was the first person to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean.
challenges.fact: Charles Lindbergh made the first solo transatlantic flight in 1927. Earhart was the first WOMAN to do so — in 1932, flying from Newfoundland to Northern Ireland in 14 hours 56 minutes. She also set the record for fastest transatlantic solo flight at that time.

challenges.question: The Long March covered approximately how many kilometres?
challenges.fact: The Long March (1934–35) covered about 9,000 km — crossing 18 mountain ranges and 24 rivers. Of the 80,000 who began, fewer than 10,000 completed it. It transformed apparent defeat into the founding myth of Communist China.

challenges.instruction: Mao's forces have repositioned. Find the decisive tactical move.
challenges.fact: The Long March was a 9,000 km strategic retreat that repositioned the Red Army — transforming apparent defeat into the foundation of eventual victory.

challenges.instruction: Lead the column through the mountain passes of the Long March
challenges.fact: The most decisive battle of the Long March was the crossing of the Luding Bridge — a chain bridge over a gorge, its planks removed, defended by machine guns. Communist soldiers crawled across the chains under fire.

challenges.question: The Long March of 1934–35 covered approximately how far, and what fraction of soldiers survived?
options: 6,000 miles; roughly one in ten survived
10,000 miles; fewer than one in a hundred survived
challenges.fact: Of 86,000 who began the Long March, roughly 8,000 arrived at Yan'an — about one in ten. The march lasted 370 days over some of the most brutal terrain in China. Mao used the ordeal to consolidate his leadership of the Communist Party.

challenges.question: How many possible settings did Turing's Bombe machine have to test for each Enigma message?
challenges.fact: The Enigma machine had 17,576 possible rotor starting positions (26×26×26). But with plugboard settings, the actual number of configurations was 158 quintillion — the Bombe exploited cribs (known plaintext) to narrow the search.

challenges.instruction: Crack the code — guess the 5-letter word hidden in the Bombe's output.
challenges.fact: Turing's Bombe worked through every possible rotor setting until the ciphertext collapsed into readable English — just as each Wordle guess collapses possibility.

challenges.instruction: Complete the Bombe circuit — the electrical circuit that cracked Enigma.
challenges.fact: Turing's Bombe was based on a Polish machine called the Bomba, which Turing and Gordon Welchman dramatically improved. At peak operation, 211 Bombe machines ran simultaneously at Bletchley Park.

challenges.instruction: Rearrange the rotor blocks to bring the cipher module to its target position.
challenges.fact: Alan Turing's bombe machine exploited a flaw in Enigma — no letter ever encrypted to itself — to narrow down rotor positions and crack the daily key.

challenges.instruction: Arrange the pseudo-code lines in the correct logical order to build working algorithms — just as Turing formalized computation.
challenges.fact: Turing's 1936 paper introduced the concept of a universal machine: a theoretical device that could simulate any algorithm by reading and writing symbols on a tape.

challenges.statement: Hillary and Tenzing reached the summit of Everest at exactly 11:30 AM on May 29, 1953.
challenges.fact: Hillary later wrote: 'We knocked the bastard off.' They spent 15 minutes on the summit — enough for photographs and a buried chocolate. The news was withheld until Queen Elizabeth II's coronation on June 2, providing a gift to the nation.

challenges.instruction: Find the route Hillary and Tenzing took through the icefall to the summit.
challenges.fact: The South Col route up Everest required navigating the Khumbu Icefall — a constantly shifting maze of ice towers. Hillary and Tenzing reached the summit on 29 May 1953.

challenges.instruction: A mountain's conical shape — calculate the surface area of the tent Hillary used at the summit camp.
challenges.fact: The Khumbu Icefall moves up to a metre per day — its seracs and crevasses constantly shift, meaning the safe route must be re-established every day. Hillary called it the crux of the entire climb.

challenges.question: Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay reached the summit of Everest on May 29, 1953. What was the first thing Hillary did at the top?
options: Photographed Tenzing holding flags, then took snow samples
challenges.fact: Hillary photographed Tenzing holding the flags of the UN, UK, Nepal and India — but there are no photos of Hillary on the summit, because Tenzing said he did not know how to use the camera. Hillary also took snow samples and searched for signs of Mallory and Irvine.

challenges.question: On which date did Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary first reach the summit of Everest?
challenges.fact: Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary summited Everest on May 29, 1953. The news reached London on June 2 — the morning of Queen Elizabeth II's coronation — making it a double celebration for Britain.

challenges.instruction: Navigate the icy slopes of Everest. Collect the oxygen key and reach the summit.
challenges.fact: Tenzing Norgay had attempted Everest six times before the 1953 expedition. His intimate knowledge of the mountain's routes was as essential as any piece of equipment.

challenges.statement: Tenzing Norgay was the first Sherpa ever to attempt Everest when he joined the 1953 expedition.
challenges.fact: Tenzing had attempted Everest six times before the 1953 expedition — first in 1935. He was chosen partly because of his unmatched experience. Sherpas had been essential to every serious Himalayan expedition since the 1920s, but rarely received equivalent recognition.

challenges.question: After the 1953 Everest summit, a dispute arose about who stepped on top first. How was it resolved?
options: A coin flip between Hillary and Tenzing
Both men publicly stated they reached the top together simultaneously
Royal Geographic Society GPS analysis settled it
Tenzing's diary proved he stepped up first
challenges.fact: Both men agreed to say they summited together and refused to reveal the order. Hillary later wrote in a private letter that he stepped up first, but Tenzing always maintained that what mattered was they did it as a team. The spirit of partnership defined how the achievement was presented to the world.

challenges.question: In what year did Mother Teresa found the Missionaries of Charity in Calcutta?
challenges.fact: Mother Teresa founded the Missionaries of Charity on 7 October 1950. Beginning with just 13 members in Calcutta, the congregation grew to over 4,500 sisters operating in 133 countries by the time of her death in 1997.

challenges.statement: Mother Teresa asked that the traditional Nobel banquet be cancelled and the money given to the poor.
challenges.fact: When Mother Teresa received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979, she asked that the $192,000 Nobel banquet fund be donated directly to the poor of Calcutta. She described the prize as recognition of 'the poorest of the poor.'

challenges.question: Arrange these milestones of Mother Teresa's life in chronological order:
items: Leaves the Loreto convent for Calcutta's slums
Founds the Missionaries of Charity
Opens Nirmal Hriday, Home for the Dying
Receives the Nobel Peace Prize
challenges.fact: Each step built on the last: leaving the convent (1948) gave her freedom to serve; the Missionaries (1950) gave her sisters; Nirmal Hriday (1952) gave the dying dignity; and the Nobel Prize (1979) gave her voice to the world.

challenges.instruction: Agra's jewellers demanded perfection — only chains of 4 or more gems matter, and diagonals count. Clear 36 gems from the 7×7 bazaar.
challenges.fact: Akbar's Mughal Empire controlled the world's richest gem pipeline: rubies from Burma, emeralds from Colombia via Portuguese Goa, sapphires from Ceylon, and diamonds from Golconda — the mine that produced the Koh-i-Noor. European merchants called Agra's Jauhari Bazaar the most magnificent market on Earth.

challenges.question: Audrey Hepburn is the only actress to have won which four major entertainment awards (EGOT)?
options: Oscar, Tony, Cannes Palme d'Or, Grammy
challenges.fact: Audrey Hepburn won an Oscar (Roman Holiday, 1953), Tony (Ondine, 1954), Emmy (Love Among Thieves, 1993), and Grammy (spoken word album, 1993) — becoming one of very few EGOT winners. She also received the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

challenges.instruction: Arrange the opening notes of 'Moon River' — the song Audrey Hepburn sang in Breakfast at Tiffany's.
challenges.fact: 'Moon River' won the 1962 Academy Award for Best Original Song. When Paramount executives suggested cutting it, Hepburn reportedly said: 'Over my dead body!' Henry Mancini's melody became her signature.

challenges.question: Arrange Audrey Hepburn's career milestones in chronological order:
items: Wins the Academy Award for Best Actress for Roman Holiday
Stars in Breakfast at Tiffany's — Givenchy's black dress becomes iconic
Appointed UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador
Receives Emmy and Grammy Awards — completing the EGOT
challenges.fact: Hepburn won the Oscar, Tony, Emmy, and Grammy — one of very few EGOT recipients. But she considered her UNICEF work her greatest achievement, visiting famine-stricken communities in Ethiopia, Sudan, Bangladesh, and Central America in her final years.

challenges.statement: Audrey Hepburn won the Academy Award for Best Actress for her role in Breakfast at Tiffany's.
challenges.fact: Hepburn won the Oscar for Roman Holiday (1953), her film debut. For Breakfast at Tiffany's (1961), she received a nomination but lost to Sophia Loren. The film's song "Moon River" won the Oscar for Best Original Song — Henry Mancini wrote it specifically for Hepburn's vocal range.

challenges.question: Where did Jane Goodall conduct her famous study of chimpanzees, beginning in 1960?
challenges.fact: Jane Goodall arrived at Gombe Stream (then a chimpanzee reserve in Tanganyika, now Tanzania) in July 1960, sent by paleoanthropologist Louis Leakey. She was 26 years old and had no formal scientific degree — but her patience and observation changed science forever.

challenges.question: What discovery by Goodall overturned the belief that only humans use tools?
options: Chimps using sticks to extract termites from mounds
Chimps using stones to crack nuts
challenges.fact: In 1960, Goodall observed chimpanzees stripping leaves from twigs to fish termites from mounds — the first recorded instance of animals making and using tools. When she reported this to Louis Leakey, he replied: 'Now we must redefine tool, redefine man, or accept chimpanzees as humans.'

challenges.question: Jane Goodall's work was notable for naming individual chimpanzees rather than numbering them. Why was this controversial?
options: It was seen as unscientific — implying chimps had personalities
Naming chimps was against the law
Other researchers wanted to name them first
challenges.fact: The scientific establishment expected researchers to remain emotionally detached and number subjects rather than name them. Goodall's insistence on naming chimps (David Greybeard, Flo, Goliath) was radical — implying each had an individual personality and inner life.

challenges.question: Jane Goodall received her PhD in Ethology from which university, without ever earning an undergraduate degree?
challenges.fact: In 1965, Goodall received her PhD from Cambridge University — becoming one of the few people admitted to a PhD program without a bachelor's degree. Cambridge made an exception because of the significance of her fieldwork at Gombe.

challenges.question: What organization did Jane Goodall found in 1977 to protect chimpanzees and their habitats?
challenges.fact: The Jane Goodall Institute (JGI), founded in 1977, works to protect chimpanzees and their habitats while improving the lives of local communities. It now operates in over 30 countries and includes the Roots & Shoots youth program.

challenges.question: Gregory Peck won the 1963 Best Actor Oscar for his portrayal of Atticus Finch. What was Atticus defending Tom Robinson against?
challenges.fact: Harper Lee based Atticus partly on her own father, a lawyer who defended two Black men in Alabama. Peck and Harper Lee became lifelong friends after the 1962 film.

challenges.instruction: Maycomb's rigid social order works like a food chain. Sort the roles: who produces, who consumes, who dominates.
challenges.fact: The AFI voted Atticus Finch the greatest movie hero of the 20th century. Peck later said the role was the one closest to his own moral convictions — he fought for civil rights throughout his career.

challenges.instruction: Atticus Finch makes his closing argument. Win enough jurors to acquit Tom Robinson.
challenges.fact: Harper Lee's novel (1960) is based partly on the 1931 Scottsboro Boys case. Despite Atticus's brilliant argument, the jury convicts — Lee's point being that moral courage alone cannot overcome structural injustice.

challenges.question: Harper Lee published only two novels in her lifetime. What was unusual about the publication of "Go Set a Watchman"?
options: It was published under a pseudonym
It was actually her first draft of Mockingbird, written decades earlier
It was found in a library archive after her death
She wrote it in a single weekend
challenges.fact: Go Set a Watchman (2015) was Lee's original manuscript, written before To Kill a Mockingbird. Her editor suggested she rewrite it from young Scout's perspective — producing Mockingbird instead. Lee said Watchman was her first book; Mockingbird was her second.

challenges.question: Michael Jackson's 'Thriller' is the best-selling album of all time. Approximately how many copies has it sold?
challenges.fact: Thriller (1982) has sold an estimated 66–70 million copies worldwide — the best-selling album in history. It produced seven Top 10 singles and won a record eight Grammy Awards in one night.

challenges.instruction: Arrange notes of Michael Jackson's iconic melodic phrase — the King of Pop's signature sound.
challenges.fact: Jackson's falsetto vocal style, rhythmic precision, and melodic invention were unprecedented in pop music. His vocal range spanned 4 octaves — from bass to soprano — and he used his voice as a percussive instrument as much as a melodic one.

challenges.question: Arrange these milestones of Michael Jackson's career in chronological order:
items: Off the Wall establishes him as a solo superstar
Thriller becomes the best-selling album in history
Moonwalk debut on the Motown 25 television special
Earth Song released — his most overtly political statement
challenges.fact: Jackson's arc — from Off the Wall's sophistication (1979) to Thriller's global domination (1982) to the moonwalk's cultural moment (1983) to Earth Song's social conscience (1995) — spanned every register of popular music. He is the only artist to have debuted a dance move that became a permanent part of world culture.

challenges.statement: Michael Jackson invented the moonwalk dance move.
challenges.fact: The sliding step had existed in various forms since the 1930s and was used by artists including Cab Calloway, Marcel Marceau, and Jeffrey Daniel. Jackson perfected and popularised it on Motown 25 (March 1983), but he credited James Brown and Fred Astaire as his inspirations — not himself as an inventor.

challenges.question: How many Michelin stars did Joël Robuchon hold at the peak of his career?
challenges.fact: At his peak, Joël Robuchon held 32 Michelin stars across his restaurants worldwide — more than any chef in history. His empire spanned Paris, Monte Carlo, Las Vegas, Tokyo, Hong Kong, and beyond, each kitchen reflecting his obsessive pursuit of perfection.

challenges.question: In 1994, Robuchon did something shocking for a famous chef. What was it?
options: He opened a fast food restaurant
He retired from cooking at the height of his fame
He moved to the United States permanently
He published all his secret recipes
challenges.fact: At age 49, at the height of his fame, Robuchon retired — closing his flagship Jamin restaurant in Paris. He said he was exhausted. He returned years later with his more casual L'Atelier concept, and earned even more stars in his second career.

challenges.question: Robuchon's most famous dish — a simple preparation that became legendary — was:
challenges.fact: Robuchon's pommes purée — made with a 1:2 ratio of potatoes to butter — became his most famous dish despite its simplicity. He believed the best cooking elevated humble ingredients to perfection, and his mashed potato proved the point.

challenges.question: Robuchon's L'Atelier restaurants were innovative for their format. What was different about them?
options: Counter seating around an open kitchen
challenges.fact: L'Atelier de Joël Robuchon (opened 2003) featured counter seating around an open kitchen — inspired by Japanese sushi bars. Diners watched chefs work, creating an intimate connection between kitchen and table. The format was revolutionary in French fine dining.

challenges.question: Robuchon held the title 'Chef of the Century' by which culinary authority?
challenges.fact: The Gault Millau guide named Joël Robuchon 'Chef of the Century' in 1990. The same guide had previously pioneered the Nouvelle Cuisine movement that transformed French cooking — making its recognition of Robuchon a major honor.

challenges.question: In which 1986 World Cup quarterfinal match did Maradona score both the 'Hand of God' and 'Goal of the Century'?
challenges.fact: In the 1986 World Cup quarterfinal, Maradona scored twice against England — first with a handball he called 'the Hand of God,' then with a dribble past five players that was later voted the Goal of the Century. Argentina won 2–1.

challenges.question: How did Maradona describe his controversial handball goal?
options: A little with the head, a little with the hand of God
challenges.fact: After the match, Maradona said the goal was scored 'a little with the head of Maradona, and a little with the hand of God.' The phrase became one of the most famous quotes in football history — a blend of cheek and genius.

challenges.question: Maradona led which club team to two Serie A titles in Italy?
challenges.fact: Maradona joined SSC Napoli in 1984 for a then-world record fee. He led the club — a southern Italian side historically overlooked — to its first (1987) and second (1990) Serie A titles, becoming a god in Naples.

challenges.question: In which Buenos Aires neighborhood did Maradona grow up in poverty?
challenges.fact: Maradona grew up in Villa Fiorito, a poor shantytown on the outskirts of Buenos Aires. His journey from dirt-floor poverty to becoming the world's best footballer became one of sport's greatest rags-to-riches stories.

challenges.question: How old was Maradona when he debuted professionally in Argentina's top division?
challenges.fact: Maradona made his professional debut for Argentinos Juniors on October 20, 1976, at just 15 years and 11 months old — one of the youngest debuts in Argentine football history. He had been identified as a prodigy at age 8.

challenges.question: Peter Arnett became internationally famous for his live TV coverage of which war?
challenges.fact: Peter Arnett broadcast live from Baghdad for CNN during the Gulf War air campaign on January 17, 1991 — the first time a war had been broadcast live on television. His reports from inside the enemy capital were watched by hundreds of millions worldwide.

challenges.question: What Pulitzer Prize-winning photograph was associated with Peter Arnett's Vietnam War coverage?
options: Raising the Flag at Iwo Jima
challenges.fact: Arnett was present and reporting when Eddie Adams took 'Saigon Execution' (1968) — one of Vietnam's most iconic photographs. Arnett himself won the Pulitzer Prize for International Reporting in 1966 for his Vietnam War coverage for the Associated Press.

challenges.question: Arnett's live Gulf War broadcast was possible because of which technology?
challenges.fact: CNN had a special four-wire telephone line and satellite uplink equipment in Baghdad's Al-Rashid Hotel. While other networks evacuated, Arnett and his CNN colleagues stayed — using this equipment to deliver the first live war coverage in television history.

challenges.question: Peter Arnett is from which country?
challenges.fact: Peter Arnett was born in Riverton, New Zealand in 1934. He began his journalism career in New Zealand before moving to Southeast Asia, where he covered the Vietnam War as a young AP reporter — launching one of journalism's most consequential careers.

challenges.question: What was controversial about Arnett's 1998 CNN interview with Osama bin Laden?
options: It was the first Western TV interview with bin Laden after he declared war on the US
He refused to ask difficult questions
challenges.fact: Arnett conducted CNN's 1997 interview with Osama bin Laden — one of the first Western television interviews after bin Laden issued his declaration of jihad against Americans. The interview was controversial for giving bin Laden a platform, but documented his stated intentions years before 9/11.

challenges.question: After returning to Apple in 1997, Jobs' first major move was to eliminate most of Apple's product lines. Why?
options: Apple was losing money on all products
He wanted to focus — fewer products done brilliantly
challenges.fact: When Jobs returned to Apple in 1997, the company had 350 products and was weeks from bankruptcy. He cut the product line to just 4 items. His philosophy: 'Deciding what not to do is as important as deciding what to do.' The iMac, announced the following year, saved the company.

challenges.question: What is the significance of Apple's 1984 Macintosh commercial?
options: It was the first TV ad for a computer
Directed by Ridley Scott, it aired during the Super Bowl and is considered one of the greatest ads ever
It was banned in most countries
challenges.fact: Directed by Ridley Scott and aired once during Super Bowl XVIII (1984), the '1984' Macintosh commercial depicted Apple as a liberator smashing IBM's Orwellian conformity. It is credited with transforming advertising into a medium for brand mythology.

challenges.question: Jobs was known for his 'reality distortion field.' What did this term mean?
options: His use of virtual reality technology
His charismatic ability to convince people to do what seemed impossible
His practice of lying about product features
His tendency to ignore financial reality
challenges.fact: The 'reality distortion field' was coined by Apple engineer Bud Tribble: Jobs could convince engineers that the impossible was achievable through sheer force of conviction, charm, and willpower — often causing them to actually achieve the impossible. It was part admiration, part alarm.

challenges.question: Steve Jobs co-founded Apple Computer with Steve Wozniak and Ronald Wayne in which year?
challenges.fact: Apple Computer was founded on April 1, 1976 in the Jobs family garage in Los Altos, California. Jobs was 21 years old. Wayne sold his 10% stake for $800 shortly after — a share that would have been worth over $100 billion by 2021.

challenges.question: In 1985, Jobs was forced out of Apple. What did he do next?
options: He founded NeXT Computer and acquired Pixar
He went to work in academia
challenges.fact: Jobs founded NeXT Computer (whose operating system later became the foundation of macOS) and purchased Pixar from George Lucas for $5 million in 1986. Pixar went on to produce Toy Story (1995) and transform animated filmmaking.

challenges.instruction: Arrange the pseudo-code in the right order. Jobs famously believed every programmer should learn to code — it teaches you how to think.
challenges.fact: Steve Jobs said: 'Everybody in this country should learn how to program a computer... because it teaches you how to think.'

challenges.instruction: Bid on landmark Silicon Valley assets. Win the starred computing relics before your rivals claim them.
challenges.fact: The early Silicon Valley era saw fierce competition over patents and prototypes. Apple's lawsuit against Xerox over the GUI and Jobs' NeXT venture shaped the modern tech landscape.
